title: Giant review
transcript:
This might be the worst case of “never meet your heroes” I've ever seen.
The wildly popular children's author Roald Dahl,
brought impeccably to life by John Lithgow,
was a raging anti-Semite, much to the horror of today's audiences
and the poor sales executive in the world of this play.
Having recently published some controversial and offensive commentary
on a book covering the Lebanese-Israeli War,
Dahl isn't in the best place to be releasing his upcoming book The Witches.
When Jessie Stone visits his home in the English countryside,
representing an American publishing company,
she's hoping for a quick conversation to clear up any misunderstandings,
a game plan for mitigating the PR crisis, and maybe an autograph for her son.
She gets so much more than she bargained for
and the afternoon becomes increasingly heated,
with Dahl continually doubling down and reaching a new pitch of monstrosity.
With the events of the play falling over the course of a single day,
it's a slow but well-earned burn.
Watching how a character reveals himself
as the stakes of a situation become higher and more personal
is incredibly captivating,
and John Lithgow's performance is rightfully the centerpiece of the whole show.
He will certainly be a front-runner for a Tony Award.
As Roald Dahl, he exudes a charming though blunt demeanor
which makes what comes out of his mouth all the more off-putting.
I did notice that the sharp focus on Dahl
and his staunch defense of his prejudices
comes at the expense of almost every other character's development.
This is far from a deal breaker though —
I didn't need the play to be perfect to feel the way I was supposed to,
which was not the best after learning what I learned.
With that, another Playbill for my collection.
reasoning: The reviewer praises John Lithgow's performance as the centerpiece, calls the play 'incredibly captivating,' and notes it as a 'slow but well-earned burn.' However, they note that other characters' development suffers due to the sharp focus on Dahl, and they didn't need the play to be 'perfect.' Overall a recommendation with caveats.
